sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 44 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?
study.intro: Twenty-six verses move from remembered victories to a national defeat the people cannot explain, a protest of loyalty, and a bold cry for God to wake and redeem.
study.context: The heading calls this a Maskil of the sons of Korah. It is a communal lament. Verses 1–8 recall how God gave Israel the land and how the people trust Him rather than their weapons; verses 9–16 describe defeat, plunder, scattering and mockery; verses 17–22 insist that the people have not abandoned the covenant; verses 23–26 call on God to wake and help. No battle is named. The psalm is unusual because it does not explain suffering as punishment for sin. Paul quotes verse 22 in Romans 8:36. The conquest language of verses 2–3 describes Israel's past and credits God, not human might; the notes do not read it as a pattern for modern wars or claims to land. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: The heading credits this Maskil, a lament for the whole nation, to the sons of Korah. Jacob is named in verse 4 as the name of the nation descended from him; his profile explains how his name came to stand for Israel. Planned paintings avoid battle gore and show landscapes, sheep, objects and anonymous groups; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Our fathers have told us
verses.heading: Faith handed down by story
verses.meaning: The heading names the sons of Korah. The psalm opens with memory passed through generations: our fathers told us what God did in the days of old. The community's faith rests on stories heard from parents and grandparents. Those stories will become the problem later in the psalm, because the present looks nothing like the past. The verse shows how faith is shared through telling, and how inherited faith must eventually face present troubles.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 6:20–23 tells parents to explain to their children what God did in Egypt, and Psalm 78:3–4 speaks of telling the next generation. Psalm 44:1 begins with that inherited memory.
explore: Heard with our ears
The community received faith through hearing. Story shaped belief.
In the days of old
The past is the measure. The psalm will contrast it with the present.
verses.reflect: What stories of God's faithfulness were passed on to you? Which will you pass on?
verses.alt: An elder points to a starry sky while children sit listening around a fire.

verses.title: Planted our fathers
verses.heading: God credited with giving the land
verses.meaning: With Your hand You drove out the nations and planted our fathers there; You crushed the peoples and cast them out. The psalm recalls Israel's entry into Canaan and credits it entirely to God. 'Planted' pictures Israel as a vine set in the soil. The language of driving out nations is hard for modern readers. Here it describes a particular moment in Israel's history and emphasizes that the land was God's gift, not Israel's achievement. It is not offered as a model for any modern conflict or territorial claim.
verses.context: Exodus 15:17 sings of God planting His people on His mountain, and Deuteronomy 9:4–5 warns Israel not to think it received the land because of its own righteousness. Psalm 80:8 also pictures Israel as a transplanted vine.
explore: Planted
Israel is pictured as a vine. Growth depends on God.
With Your hand
The action is God's, not Israel's. The emphasis is on gift, not achievement.
verses.reflect: What do you have that you received rather than earned? How does that shape your gratitude?
verses.alt: A young grapevine is set into terraced soil on a hillside.

verses.title: Not by their sword
verses.heading: Victory by God's favor
verses.meaning: For it was not by their sword that they took the land; their arm did not bring them victory. It was by Your right hand, Your arm, and the light of Your face, because You favored them. The verse insists that military strength did not win the land. God's right hand and arm, images of power, and the light of His face, an image of favor, were the reason. The last phrase is key: because You favored them. The gift rested on God's grace, not on Israel's might or merit.
verses.context: Numbers 6:25 blesses, 'May the LORD make His face shine upon you,' and Joshua 24:12 says it was 'not by your sword or bow.' Psalm 44:3 joins God's power and His favor.
explore: Not by their sword
Human strength is not the source. The psalm denies self-credit.
The light of Your face
God's face shining means favor. Grace explains the victory.
verses.reflect: Where are you tempted to credit your own strength for what God has given?
verses.alt: A sword lies unused in long grass as sunlight floods a valley.

verses.title: You are my King
verses.heading: God who ordains victory for Jacob
verses.meaning: You are my King, O God, who ordains victories for Jacob. The voice shifts to the singular for a moment: 'my King.' Perhaps a leader speaks for the people. God is the true King, and He commands or ordains deliverance for Jacob, a name for the nation descended from the patriarch. The verse turns history into present confession. The same God who acted in the past is the King now.
verses.context: Jacob was renamed Israel in Genesis 32:28, and his name often stands for the whole people. Psalm 74:12 says, 'God is my King from of old.' Psalm 44:4 applies that kingship to the present.
explore: My King
God is confessed as ruler. The singular makes it personal.
Ordains victories
God commands deliverance. Salvation is His decision.
verses.reflect: What would it mean to confess God as your King in the situation you face?
verses.alt: A gold crown rests on a cushion before an empty carved throne.

verses.title: Through Your name
verses.heading: Strength drawn from God
verses.meaning: Through You we repel our foes; through Your name we trample our enemies. The people speak again. Their confidence is not in themselves but in God and His name. 'Through You' is repeated for emphasis. The language is military, describing defense and victory. The verse affirms that whatever strength the people have comes from God. It continues the theme of verse 3 into the present tense.
verses.context: Psalm 20:7 says, 'Some trust in chariots, but we trust in the name of the LORD,' and Psalm 60:12 says, 'With God we will perform with valor.' Psalm 44:5 shares that confidence.
explore: Through Your name
God's name represents His character and presence. It is the source of strength.
Repel our foes
The image is defense. The people trust God to protect them.
verses.reflect: What challenge could you face 'through God' rather than through your own strength?
verses.alt: A line of round shields stands along a wall with a banner above.

verses.title: Not my bow
verses.heading: Rejecting trust in weapons
verses.meaning: For I do not trust in my bow, nor does my sword save me. The singular voice returns, perhaps the king or leader. He refuses to place trust in his weapons. This does not mean he has no weapons, but that they are not his savior. The verse echoes the earlier insistence that the fathers did not win by the sword. Trust is a matter of where the heart rests.
verses.context: 1 Samuel 17:47 records David saying, 'It is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves,' and Hosea 1:7 promises deliverance 'not by bow or sword.' Psalm 44:6 makes that a personal confession.
explore: I do not trust
Trust is the issue. Weapons cannot be the foundation.
My sword
The sword is real but not saving. Salvation belongs to God.
verses.reflect: What 'bow and sword' are you tempted to trust instead of God?
verses.alt: An unstrung bow hangs on a peg in a quiet room.

verses.title: You put them to shame
verses.heading: God's past saving acts
verses.meaning: For You save us from our enemies; You put those who hate us to shame. The reason for not trusting weapons is given: God saves. The shame falls on those who hate Israel, meaning their plans fail and they are exposed. This verse completes the confident first section. It sets up the shocking turn that comes in verse 9, where the people themselves will be shamed.
verses.context: Psalm 25:3 prays that none who wait for God will be ashamed, and Psalm 44:15 will later say shame covers the speaker's face. Verse 7 shows the expected pattern before it breaks.
explore: You save us
God is the active Savior. The people depend on Him.
Put to shame
The enemies' plans fail. They are exposed as wrong.
verses.reflect: Where have you seen God save in the past? How does that shape your hope now?
verses.alt: Abandoned enemy tents sag on an empty plain at sunrise.

verses.title: Boasted all day long
verses.heading: Praise as the people's boast
verses.meaning: In God we have boasted all day long, and Your name we will praise forever. Selah. The people's only boast is God. They have spoken of Him all day and promise to praise Him forever. Selah, a musical or liturgical marker, pauses the song. This is the high point of confidence. The next verse will bring a sharp turn. The pause invites the listener to feel the weight of what comes next.
verses.context: Jeremiah 9:24 says, 'Let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me,' and 1 Corinthians 1:31 repeats the idea. The Selah here marks the hinge between praise and lament.
explore: Boasted in God
The people's pride is in God, not themselves. Their confidence rests on Him.
Selah
The marker pauses the song. The next section reverses the tone.
verses.reflect: What do you boast in? How could God become your boast?
verses.alt: Trumpets and cymbals rest on temple steps after a festival.

verses.title: But You have rejected us
verses.heading: The sudden turn to defeat
verses.meaning: But You have rejected and humbled us; You no longer go forth with our armies. The tone breaks. After boasting in God, the people say He has rejected them. He no longer marches with them, as He once did with the ark. The 'but' is jarring. The psalm does not soften this. It names the experience of defeat as if God has stepped away. This honesty is part of biblical faith.
verses.context: Numbers 10:35 records the ark going out before Israel, and 1 Samuel 4:3–11 tells of a defeat even when the ark was present. Psalm 60:10 repeats the complaint that God no longer goes out with the armies.
explore: Rejected and humbled
The people feel cast off. Their pride is brought low.
No longer go forth
God's presence seems absent. The defeat feels like abandonment.
verses.reflect: Have you ever felt God stepped away when you needed Him? How could you say so honestly?
verses.alt: A torn banner lies in the mud on an empty road.

verses.title: Plundered
verses.heading: Retreat and loss
verses.meaning: You have made us retreat from the foe, and those who hate us have plundered us. The defeat is described concretely. The people retreat, and their enemies take their goods. Notice the speaker still addresses God: 'You have made us retreat.' The psalm holds God responsible because God is sovereign. It does not let go of Him even while blaming Him. Lament can sound like accusation and still be prayer.
verses.context: Leviticus 26:17 and Deuteronomy 28:25 describe defeat as a covenant curse, but this psalm will insist the people have kept the covenant (44:17). That tension makes the lament sharper.
explore: Retreat
The people turn back before their enemies. It is a humiliating loss.
Plundered
Their goods are taken. Defeat is economic as well as military.
verses.reflect: Have you ever lost what you depended on? How could you speak to God about it?
verses.alt: Empty storage jars lie tipped over in a ransacked courtyard.

verses.title: Sheep to be devoured
verses.heading: Scattered among the nations
verses.meaning: You have given us up as sheep to be devoured; You have scattered us among the nations. The image changes to sheep handed over to predators. Israel is God's flock, so this means the Shepherd seems to have abandoned them. Scattering among nations suggests exile or flight. The verse describes vulnerability and displacement. It anticipates verse 22, where the sheep image returns.
verses.context: Psalm 23 pictures God as Shepherd, and Ezekiel 34:5–6 describes sheep scattered with no shepherd. Psalm 44:11 feels that the Shepherd has given them up.
explore: As sheep
Israel is God's flock. Without the Shepherd they feel defenseless before predators.
Scattered
The people are dispersed. Exile or flight is implied.
verses.reflect: Where do you feel scattered or exposed? How could you bring that to God the Shepherd?
verses.alt: A flock scatters across a rocky hillside under a dark sky.

verses.title: Sold for nothing
verses.heading: God seeming to gain nothing
verses.meaning: You sell Your people for nothing; no profit do You gain from their sale. The people feel cheaply sold, like goods given away. Even a seller usually gains something, but here God seems to gain nothing. The verse is bold. It suggests the people feel worthless in God's eyes. Isaiah 52:3 later answers, 'You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.' The complaint will be answered by redemption.
verses.context: Isaiah 52:3 promises redemption for a people sold for nothing, and Judges 2:14 describes God selling Israel to enemies. Psalm 44:26 ends by asking God to redeem.
explore: For nothing
The people feel undervalued. The complaint is blunt.
No profit
God seems to gain nothing. The loss seems pointless.
verses.reflect: Have you felt worthless or overlooked? How might God's redemption answer that?
verses.alt: A marketplace scale holds a single empty pan raised high.

verses.title: A reproach to neighbors
verses.heading: Mockery from surrounding peoples
verses.meaning: You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us. The defeat brings social shame. Nearby peoples laugh. In the ancient world, a nation's defeat was often read as its god's weakness, so the mockery also targets God. The verse names the pain of public humiliation. It is honest about how shame compounds loss.
verses.context: Psalm 79:4 uses nearly the same words, and Nehemiah 4:1–4 records neighbors mocking Jerusalem's rebuilding. Shame before neighbors is a recurring biblical lament.
explore: A reproach
The people become an object of scorn. Their defeat is public.
Those around us
The mockery is local and constant. Shame surrounds them.
verses.reflect: Have you experienced public embarrassment? How could you bring that shame to God?
verses.alt: Neighbors point and laugh from a rooftop across the street.

verses.title: A byword
verses.heading: A name used as an insult
verses.meaning: You have made us a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples. The mockery spreads beyond neighbors to nations. A byword is a name used in proverbs or insults, as in 'as cursed as Israel.' People shake their heads in contempt, a gesture implied by 'laughingstock.' The verse describes how a people's suffering can become a joke for others. The repetition across verses 13–14 emphasizes the depth of humiliation.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 28:37 warns of becoming a byword among the nations, and Jeremiah 24:9 uses the same language. Psalm 44:14 feels that curse fulfilled despite covenant faithfulness.
explore: A byword
Israel's name becomes an insult. Others use it in proverbs.
A laughingstock
Others shake their heads. The defeat is ridiculed widely.
verses.reflect: Have you ever felt like a joke to others? How does God see you?
verses.alt: Caravan merchants gesture and laugh at a crossroads under palm trees.

verses.title: Shame covers my face
verses.heading: Personal disgrace
verses.meaning: All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face. The voice becomes singular again. The leader or a representative speaker feels the disgrace personally and constantly. Shame covering the face pictures someone unable to look up. The verse carries the communal humiliation into one person's experience. It runs into verse 16, which names the cause.
verses.context: Psalm 69:7 says, 'Shame has covered my face,' and Jeremiah 51:51 laments being covered with shame. Psalm 44:15 makes the people's disgrace personal.
explore: All day long
The disgrace never leaves. It follows the speaker through every hour of the day.
Covered my face
The person cannot look up. Shame is visible on the face for everyone to see.
verses.reflect: What shame do you carry before others? How could you bring it to God?
verses.alt: A head veil drapes over a bowed figure seated against a wall.

verses.title: The voice of the scorner
verses.heading: The cause of disgrace
verses.meaning: At the voice of the scorner and reviler, because of the enemy, bent on revenge. This verse completes the sentence from verse 15. The shame comes from hearing scornful voices and from an enemy seeking revenge. The people feel exposed to constant verbal attack. 'Bent on revenge' describes a hostile power determined to repay. The psalm names the source of the disgrace before turning to protest innocence.
verses.context: Psalm 74:10 asks, 'How long will the enemy mock?' and Psalm 8:2 speaks of silencing the enemy and avenger. Psalm 44:16 hears that enemy's voice.
explore: Scorner and reviler
The attack is verbal. Insulting words carry the shame into the people's hearing.
Bent on revenge
The enemy seeks payback. Their hostility is deliberate, not an accident of war.
verses.reflect: What voices shame you? How might God silence or answer them?
verses.alt: Rams' horns blare from a hostile camp on a distant ridge.

verses.title: We have not forgotten You
verses.heading: A protest of covenant loyalty
verses.meaning: All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant. This verse turns the psalm. The people insist that their suffering is not because they abandoned God. They have kept the covenant. This is rare in Scripture, where national defeat is often explained as judgment for sin. The psalm refuses that explanation here. It shows that suffering can come to the faithful, an insight shared with Job.
verses.context: Job 1:1 and 1:22 describe Job's integrity in suffering, and the prophets often explain defeat as judgment (2 Kings 17:7). Psalm 44:17 insists this time is different.
explore: Not forgotten You
The people claim faithfulness. Their memory of God is intact.
Betrayed Your covenant
They deny breaking the covenant. The suffering seems undeserved.
verses.reflect: Have you suffered even when you were trying to be faithful? How could you bring that confusion to God?
verses.alt: A covenant scroll lies carefully rolled and tied on a stone shelf.

verses.title: Our steps have not strayed
verses.heading: Hearts and steps loyal
verses.meaning: Our hearts have not turned back; our steps have not strayed from Your path. The protest continues. Hearts, the inner life, and steps, the outer life, have both stayed faithful. 'Your path' is the way of the covenant. The people do not claim sinless perfection, but they deny the kind of rejection of God that would explain such defeat. The verse sets up the confusion of verse 19.
verses.context: Psalm 119:51 says, 'I have not turned from Your law,' and Job 23:11 says, 'My foot has held fast to His steps.' Psalm 44:18 makes the same claim for the community.
explore: Hearts and steps
Inner and outer loyalty are both claimed. The whole life is involved.
Your path
The covenant is the road. The people insist they stayed on it.
verses.reflect: Where are you trying to walk God's path faithfully? How does it feel when hardship comes anyway?
verses.alt: Footprints run straight along a sandy road marked with cairns.

verses.title: The lair of jackals
verses.heading: Crushed in desolate darkness
verses.meaning: But You have crushed us in the lair of jackals; You have covered us with deepest darkness. The protest is followed by more lament. Jackals lived in ruins and desolate places, so the image pictures the people crushed in a wasteland. 'Deepest darkness' is the same phrase as 'the valley of the shadow of death' in Psalm 23:4. The people feel crushed and covered by deathly gloom despite their faithfulness.
verses.context: Jeremiah 9:11 says Jerusalem will become a lair of jackals, and Psalm 23:4 uses the same word for deepest darkness. Psalm 44:19 joins both images.
explore: Lair of jackals
The image is of ruined, desolate places. The people feel abandoned there.
Deepest darkness
The darkness is deathly. It uses the same word as the shadow of death in Psalm 23.
verses.reflect: What darkness covers you now? How could you remember God is present even there?
verses.alt: Jackals prowl among the ruined walls of a deserted town at dusk.

verses.title: If we had forgotten
verses.heading: Testing the protest
verses.meaning: If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god, the psalm begins a conditional sentence that continues in verse 21. To spread out hands was a gesture of prayer. The people imagine a scenario in which they had worshiped other gods. That would explain the suffering. But they deny it. The verse shows how seriously they consider whether they are at fault.
verses.context: 1 Kings 8:22 shows Solomon spreading his hands toward heaven in prayer, and Exodus 20:3 forbids other gods. Psalm 44:20 tests whether idolatry explains the defeat.
explore: Forgotten the name
Forgetting God's name means abandoning Him. The people deny it.
A foreign god
Idolatry would explain judgment. They insist it did not happen.
verses.reflect: When things go wrong, how do you honestly search your heart without assuming every trouble is punishment?
verses.alt: A toppled clay idol lies untouched in the dust outside a house.

verses.title: He knows the secrets
verses.heading: God who sees the heart
verses.meaning: Would not God have discovered, since He knows the secrets of the heart? The sentence from verse 20 is completed. If the people had secretly turned to other gods, God would know. The appeal is to God's perfect knowledge. They invite His examination. This shows confidence that their protest of loyalty will stand before a God who sees everything. Confidence before God's searching gaze is the opposite of hiding.
verses.context: 1 Samuel 16:7 says, 'The LORD looks on the heart,' and Psalm 139:1 says, 'O LORD, You have searched me and known me.' Psalm 44:21 appeals to that knowledge.
explore: Would not God discover?
The question appeals to God's knowledge. Hidden sin cannot stay hidden.
Secrets of the heart
God knows inner motives. The people trust Him to judge truly.
verses.reflect: Are you willing to invite God to search your heart? What might that look like?
verses.alt: A lamp lights the hidden corners of an inner storeroom.

verses.title: For Your sake
verses.heading: Suffering because of loyalty
verses.meaning: Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered. Here the psalm reaches a startling conclusion: the people suffer not because they turned from God but because of Him. Their loyalty makes them targets. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 8:36, then declares that nothing can separate believers from God's love. The verse gives words to suffering for faith.
verses.context: Romans 8:35–39 quotes this verse and then insists that in all these things we are more than conquerors. 1 Peter 4:14 also speaks of being insulted for Christ's name. Psalm 44:22 becomes a text for faithful suffering.
explore: For Your sake
Their suffering is because of their loyalty. Faith makes them targets.
Sheep to be slaughtered
The sheep image returns. They feel helpless and condemned.
verses.reflect: Have you ever paid a cost for faith? How does Romans 8 add hope to that?
verses.alt: A lamb rests quietly in a stone pen at dusk.

verses.title: Wake up, O Lord!
verses.heading: A bold cry for God to act
verses.meaning: Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise! Do not reject us forever. This is one of the boldest prayers in Scripture. The people call on God to wake up, as if He were asleep. Psalm 121:4 says God never sleeps, so this is not a theological claim but an expression of how it feels. The cry 'Arise!' echoes the words spoken when the ark set out (Numbers 10:35). The people dare to demand God's action.
verses.context: Numbers 10:35 records Moses saying, 'Rise up, O LORD!' when the ark moved, and Psalm 121:4 says God neither slumbers nor sleeps. Mark 4:38 records the disciples waking Jesus during a storm.
explore: Why are You sleeping?
The question expresses how it feels. God seems inactive.
Arise!
The cry echoes the ark's march. The people ask God to lead again.
verses.reflect: What would it mean to pray boldly, even demanding God's help?
verses.alt: A watchman's horn rests on the parapet of a city wall at first light.

verses.title: Why hide Your face?
verses.heading: Questioning God's absence
verses.meaning: Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression? The people ask why God seems to hide. To hide the face means withdrawing favor, the opposite of verse 3's 'light of Your face.' They ask why He forgets their suffering. The question shows the agony of feeling unseen by the God who once shone on them. Lament keeps asking rather than walking away.
verses.context: Psalm 13:1 asks, 'How long will You hide Your face?' and Psalm 44:3 recalled the light of God's face. Deuteronomy 31:17 speaks of God hiding His face in judgment, which deepens the confusion here.
explore: Hide Your face
Favor seems withdrawn. The people feel unseen by the God who once shone on them.
Forget our affliction
God seems to overlook their suffering. They ask why.
verses.reflect: Where do you feel God is hiding? How could you keep asking instead of turning away?
verses.alt: A cloud covers the sun over a dim village of flat roofs.

verses.title: Sunk to the dust
verses.heading: Utter humiliation
verses.meaning: For our soul has sunk to the dust; our bodies cling to the earth. The people describe themselves as flattened. The image is of lying face down in the dust, a posture of mourning or defeat. Soul and body are both brought low. This is the lowest point of the psalm. From here they make their final request.
verses.context: Psalm 119:25 says, 'My soul cleaves to the dust,' and Joshua 7:6 shows mourning with dust on heads. Psalm 44:25 describes the people flattened in defeat.
explore: Sunk to the dust
The soul is bowed down completely. Despair is total.
Cling to the earth
The body lies face down. The posture is mourning and defeat.
verses.reflect: When you feel completely flattened, what could you still say to God?
verses.alt: A trampled field of grain lies flat after a storm.

verses.title: Redeem us
verses.heading: Appeal to loving devotion
verses.meaning: Rise up; be our help! Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion. The psalm ends with a final appeal. The people ask God to rise and help and to redeem them. They do not base the request on their faithfulness, though they claimed it. They base it on God's loving devotion, His covenant love. The psalm ends without resolution, but it ends in prayer that rests on God's character.
verses.context: Isaiah 52:3 answers the complaint of being sold for nothing with redemption, and Psalm 6:4 also asks God to save 'because of Your loving devotion.' Psalm 44:26 rests the whole plea on God's covenant love.
explore: Rise up
The cry from verse 23 returns. God is asked to act.
Your loving devotion
The ground of hope is God's love. It is not the people's merit.
verses.reflect: What would it mean to rest your hope on God's loving devotion rather than your own record?
verses.alt: Dawn light breaks across a broken bridge being repaired with new timber.
